questions.worked_solution:
The reference angle is the acute angle that $\theta $ makes with the $x$-axis.

First, we create a right-triangle by drawing a vertical line from $P$ to the $x$-axis.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14225277/assets/403edda1121bb4a647a52fcff755659ab1f9fe2ea310572b13be423cef4d6db9.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14225277/assets/38a60a712b18a4b9575ed812f8bd184a56ae5969fe865b9edc12f2b0faccd48f.png)

We know that the hypotenuse has a length of $1$ because it is a radius of the unit circle. 

Now, using the triangle above, we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡{\theta }_{R}=\frac{0.26}{1}=0.26.
$$

Now, we compute the angle ${\theta }_{R}$ using the inverse cosine:

$$
{\theta }_{R}=\operatorname{arccos}⁡(0.26)≈{75}^{∘}
$$

questions.problem: An angle $\theta $ in the coordinate plane (measured in the usual way) has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}={20}^{∘}.$ Which of the following cannot be $\theta ?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's remind ourselves of the relationship between ${\theta }_{R}$ and $\theta .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14225277/assets/a2d02d14edf25a59eceb842a2cc902f07a29754f0978ec56a8293e16698ec383.png)

Using ${\theta }_{R}={20}^{∘},$ let's calculate all possible values of $\theta .$

- If $\theta $ lies in the first quadrant, then $\theta ={\theta }_{R}={20}^{∘}.$

- If $\theta $ lies in the second quadrant, then $\theta ={180}^{∘}-{\theta }_{R}={180}^{∘}-{20}^{∘}={160}^{∘}.$

- If $\theta $ lies in the third quadrant, then $\theta ={180}^{∘}+{\theta }_{R}={180}^{∘}+{20}^{∘}={200}^{∘}.$

- If $\theta $ lies in the fourth quadrant, then $\theta ={360}^{∘}-{\theta }_{R}={360}^{∘}-{20}^{∘}={340}^{∘}.$

Therefore, $\theta $ cannot be equal to ${260}^{∘}.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating a Reference Angle in Radians
canonical_examples.problem: If the angle $\theta = \dfrac{11\pi}{9}$ is represented in the coordinate plane in the usual way, then what is its reference angle?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To help us to visualize the angle, we first convert the measure of the angle into degrees. 

To convert the measure of an angle in radians to an equivalent measure in degrees, we multiply the measure in radians by $\dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi}.$ This gives

$$
\left(\dfrac{11\pi} {9}\right) \cdot \left(\dfrac {180^\circ} {\pi}\right) = 
	220^\circ.
$$

Therefore $\dfrac{11\pi} {9}$ is equivalent to $220^\circ,$ which lies in the third quadrant.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14225277/assets/964e1116b6f9273321faf21f3f30c325ec81f49622eab951bc6a54823f3c7079.png)

The reference angle, denoted $\theta_R,$  is the angle that $\theta$ makes with the $x$-axis.

As $\theta$ is in the third quadrant, its reference angle is given by

$$
\theta_R = \theta - \pi.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\frac{11\pi }{9}-\pi =\frac{2\pi }{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14225277/assets/75717526542bddffb22bbf8ca2593187fea84724fdd107b1327c049e6495a57b.png)

The diagram above shows a unit circle and the angle $\theta$ is measured in the usual way. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $0.74,$ calculate the reference angle $\theta_R$ in degrees to the nearest integer.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we create a right triangle by drawing a vertical line from $P$ to the $x$-axis.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14225277/assets/5e3cf6be5c87565683466ecf91646e3587accc41cd4d1774ec6aaed007f1e809.png)

So we have the following triangle, where $\theta_R$ is the reference angle of $\theta.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14225277/assets/51bfc8624d27c386ceaaea38ab99ac1d96ed880e5674b90c9dd00b15579b0d6a.png)

We know that the hypotenuse has a length of $1$ because it is a radius of the unit circle. 

Now, using the triangle above, we have

$$
\cos \theta_R = \dfrac{0.74}{1}  = 0.74.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\theta_R = \arccos\left(0.74\right) \approx 42^\circ.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding All of the Angles With a Given Reference Angle
canonical_examples.problem:
An angle $\theta$ in the coordinate plane (measured in the usual way) has a reference angle $\theta_R = 30^\circ.$ Which of the following cannot be $\theta?$

I. $30^\circ$

II. $150^\circ$

III. $240^\circ$

IV. $330^\circ$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's remind ourselves of the relationship between $\theta_R$ and $\theta.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14225277/assets/0af4dfb696fc96a64d470ffe4561be7d039788cb83b651e48bfd4ad2d4b86fc5.png)

Using $\theta_R = 30^\circ,$ let's calculate all possible values of $\theta.$

- If $\theta$ lies in the first quadrant, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta ={\theta }_{R}={30}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $\theta$ lies in the second quadrant, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & ={180}^{∘}-{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={180}^{∘}-{30}^{∘} \\  & ={150}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $\theta$ lies in the third quadrant, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & ={180}^{∘}+{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={180}^{∘}+{30}^{∘} \\  & ={210}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $\theta$ lies in the fourth quadrant, then

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & ={360}^{∘}-{\theta }_{R} \\  & ={360}^{∘}-{30}^{∘} \\  & ={330}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\theta$ cannot be equal to $240^\circ.$
